real_s3.explanation: The unit responds to frontal, upright canine faces with both eyes and the eye/brow region fully in view, at moderate-to-large scale. It extends more weakly to frontal faces of other furry mammals such as the lesser panda, not only to wild canids.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to frontal, upright canine faces with both eyes and the eye/brow region fully in view, at moderate-to-large scale. It extends more weakly to frontal faces of other furry mammals such as the lesser panda, not only to wild canids.
parsed.evidence: Within classes, orientation and eye visibility separate activity most strongly: frontal faces score d +0.81 (98th percentile) and both eyes visible score +0.84 (97th), while profiles score -1.23 and one eye visible scores -0.86. Simply having a dog present barely matters (d +0.02), and among photos without a canine face, other furry mammal faces score d +0.50 (94th percentile); the lesser panda is also one of the top classes.
parsed.missing_data: Activations on frontal faces of non-canid mammals such as cats, bears and primates, plus more wild canid photos, to tell whether this is a dog-face unit or a general frontal-mammal-face unit.

null_s3.explanation: The unit responds broadly to dogs, especially small long-haired terriers, toy breeds and spitz/shepherd types, and extends weakly to a dog-like furry face, the lesser panda. It does not appear to respond specifically to the frontal eye/brow region.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds broadly to dogs, especially small long-haired terriers, toy breeds and spitz/shepherd types, and extends weakly to a dog-like furry face, the lesser panda. It does not appear to respond specifically to the frontal eye/brow region.
parsed.evidence: Eleven of the 12 top classes are dog breeds and the 12th is the lesser panda, but within those classes the face-detail questions barely matter: eye/brow visibility is at separation percentile 1, uprightness at 4, eye visibility at 7, and frontal faces are actually slightly less active (d -0.22) than three-quarter views (d +0.34, percentile 91). That suggests a class-level dog signal rather than the claimed eye-region detector.
parsed.missing_data: Activations on non-top classes with canine faces (wolves, foxes, coyotes) and on cropped or masked images isolating the eye region versus the body and fur would most change this answer.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds mainly to dogs at the class level, especially many dog breeds plus a related furry mammal (lesser panda). Within those classes, the specific face-related properties claimed (upright face, eye/upper-face region) do not explain its activity.
parsed.evidence: The top classes are almost all dog breeds plus lesser panda, which supports a dog-centered unit with a related extension. parsed.missing_data: Activations on non-dog classes (wolves, foxes, cats, other animals) and spatial activation maps would show whether the unit is face-specific or responds to dog/fur texture more broadly.
